title: Evidence, Inference, and Opinion: A Better Research Habit
content:
“The export took forty seconds” is an observation. “The server was overloaded” is an inference. “The service is too slow for our workflow” is an opinion informed by requirements. A useful research note can contain all three, provided readers can tell which is which and follow the evidence behind the inference.

This distinction is practical when researching tools, reading studies, investigating incidents, or preparing a recommendation. The framework below is an editorial note-taking method. It does not replace specialist methods for clinical research, statistical analysis, or legal fact-finding.

Write observations narrowly

Record what you actually encountered, including the conditions. “A sample file exported as CSV from the trial account” is more precise than “The product supports all our reporting.” The first statement describes an event. The second jumps over file size, permissions, field coverage, repeatability, and plan limits.

Attach the source location and date to observations that may change. For a technical document, include the product or API version if available. For a direct experiment, describe the input and environment without exposing sensitive data. A colleague should be able to understand what would need repeating to check the observation.

W3C's PROV overview describes provenance in terms of the things, activities, and people involved in producing information. You do not need to implement its formal model to adopt the practical habit: retain where a claim came from and how it was transformed into your note.

Expose the bridge from evidence to inference

An inference explains what observations may mean. State the assumption connecting them. If several pages load slowly, server overload is one possibility; an unstable connection, heavy client code, or a regional path may also explain the pattern. Name plausible alternatives before treating a convenient explanation as established fact.

Use language that matches the strength of evidence. “Consistent with,” “suggests,” and “not yet distinguished from” can express a real boundary when accompanied by specifics. They should not become decorative hedges around an otherwise unsupported assertion. Say which additional observation would increase or reduce confidence.

For quantitative research, identify the population, comparison, outcome, and missing information. Cochrane's risk-of-bias chapter illustrates a structured approach in randomized trials, including written justification for judgments. Its specialist tool is not a universal scoring system for websites, but the demand for justified judgments is a useful discipline.

A hypothetical software comparison

Imagine a hypothetical team comparing two document services. In a trial account, Service A exports a sample folder with filenames intact. Service B exports the same kind of sample but changes some filenames. Those are observations about a specific sample and account state, not claims about every possible export.

The researcher infers that Service A may require less cleanup for this team's archive. They record the assumption that the larger archive uses similar filename patterns. They also note an unresolved question: whether either service preserves links between documents. That missing check could reverse the apparent advantage.

The recommendation says, “Prefer A for a limited pilot because filename preservation fits the current archive, subject to link preservation and full-volume export checks.” This is an opinion tied to requirements. It is stronger than “A is better” because it tells the reader both why the choice makes sense and when it should be reconsidered.

Keep disagreement productive

When two sources disagree, compare their scope before choosing a winner. They may describe different versions, populations, time periods, or outcomes. A benchmark of a development build does not directly contradict a production user's report from a different environment. Preserve both claims until their conditions are clear.

Look for the original document behind summaries. A secondhand article can be helpful for discovery, but it may omit qualifications or repeat another writer's mistake. Record whether you inspected the primary source yourself. If you could not access it, state that limitation rather than using a confident citation to imply verification.

Avoid counting multiple copies of the same claim as independent support. Ten pages repeating one announcement still trace back to one announcement. A provenance note makes that dependence visible. Seek different kinds of evidence when the decision matters: documentation, a reproducible example, and a relevant independent observation may answer different questions.

Make uncertainty useful to the decision

Not every unknown deserves another day of research. Rank uncertainties by whether they could change the choice and how costly they are to resolve. An unverified export limit may be decisive for an archive migration. An unknown cosmetic preference may not matter to the immediate task. Explain why you stopped, not just where.

Keep a short revision history for consequential recommendations. When new information arrives, update the conclusion and note which assumption changed. This is more useful than quietly replacing an old confident statement, because future readers can understand how the decision evolved.

For a final handoff, include one sentence stating the current conclusion and another stating its strongest limitation. Keep the supporting observation sheet nearby rather than embedding every detail in the recommendation. This lets a busy reader act while preserving an inspectable route back to the evidence and the assumptions that shaped your judgment.

Research-note checklist

  • Label direct observations, inferences, and recommendations.
  • Record source, date, scope, and relevant version.
  • Preserve the original context behind a quotation or number.
  • State assumptions and competing explanations.
  • Do not count repeated announcements as independent evidence.
  • Identify unresolved questions that could change the choice.
  • Keep opinions tied to the user's actual requirements.
  • Revise conclusions openly when evidence changes.
excerpt: Separate observations, inferences, and opinions in research notes, preserve provenance, and make recommendations whose assumptions and uncertainty are visible.
